title: How profitable is retail options trading?
summary: Summarises studies finding retail options trades are tiny, speculative, pay huge spreads, lose billions after costs, and enrich wholesalers via payment for order flow.

assertions.quote: From November 2019 through June 2021, after trading costs, retail trades lost more than $4 billion!
retail investors’ motives for trading appear to be gambling and entertainment
bid-ask spreads on options exchanges are considerably higher than those on stock exchanges
PFOF creates an incentive for brokerages to encourage investors to trade more, and to trade assets with larger spreads
the dollar trading volume in options grew by 143 percent from November 2019 to July 2021
Retail investors are less likely to exercise their options optimally, failing to exercise them prior to the ex-dividend date

verdicts.note: Documented in several studies of early-exercise behaviour around dividends.

Higher retail trading in a contract strongly predicts the fraction of in-the-money calls left suboptimally unexercised on cum-dividend dates, and the effect grows for the most profitable-to-exercise contracts, pointing to investor mistakes.

assertions.quote: wholesalers (like the casinos in Las Vegas) are extracting billions in spreads
investors may accept low returns and high volatility because they are attracted to high positive skewness

verdicts.note: The skewness or lottery preference is a robust asset-pricing finding across stocks, options and other assets.

Crypto adoption responds less to price rises in more risk-averse countries and UK survey evidence cites 'a gamble that could make or lose money' as a main reason for buying, consistent with lottery-style motives, but expected returns are not measured.
